processing: Taproots of plants at least two years old are dug, sliced, dried for about two weeks and oven-roasted. Unroasted root is also sometimes called dandelion tea and tastes different.
harvest_season: Roots are dug in spring for a sweeter, less bitter flavour, or in autumn for a richer and more bitter one.
appearance_dry: Chopped root pieces, roasted to a dark coffee brown.
appearance_liquor: Dark brown and coffee-like when roasted.
appearance_wet: Softened, dark brown chunks of root.
taste_profile: Coffee-like when roasted, with a toasty bitterness; spring roots lean sweeter and autumn roots richer and more bitter.

brewing.notes: About a teaspoon of roasted root steeped for around 10 minutes. Many people add cream and sugar, as with coffee.

vintage_note: No vintages: it is sold year-round as roasted root, ground or in bags, or made at home. The dig matters more than the year, with spring and autumn roots tasting different, but packaging rarely says which. Check whether the root is roasted, since the name covers both.
description:
Dandelion tea, called mindeulle-cha in Korean, is a tisane of dandelion root, usually roasted. The roasted version looks and tastes enough like coffee that it is often called dandelion coffee. It is made in many countries, and Korea is only one home for it.

The plant must be at least two years old, and older plants with a thicker taproot are preferred. The roots are sliced, dried and then roasted, and that roast creates the coffee character. If you forage, make sure you have a true dandelion: a ground-level rosette of deeply toothed leaves and hollow stems, unlike catsear or hawksbeard.

Steep a teaspoon for about ten minutes. It is one infusion, dark and pleasantly bitter, and it takes cream and sugar well. Spring-dug root is sweeter and autumn-dug root is more bitter.

Buy it for the taste. There is no solid evidence that dandelion root treats any medical condition, whatever the packet implies, and it can occasionally cause stomach upset, heartburn or allergic reactions.
history:
The plant has a long record of use in the ancient Mediterranean and in Chinese medicine, but the roasted drink is documented much later. Susanna Moodie described making dandelion coffee in her 1852 memoir Roughing It in the Bush, crediting an 1830s article by a Dr Harrison in the New York Albion.

It has mostly been a stand-in when coffee was scarce or dear: Confederate soldiers drank it in the American Civil War, a 1919 note lists it as a cheap source of coffee, and it was widely drunk in Germany during the Second World War.
